questions.q: What is the actual governance problem an architecture review board (ARB) exists to solve, per this lesson?
options: It exists purely to satisfy a compliance checkbox with no real technical purpose
A single architect has blind spots and incentives to defend their own design, so a board distributes judgment across several people before an expensive decision is locked in
It replaces the need for any architect to design a system in the first place
It exists only to slow down projects that are already over budget
questions.explain: An ARB distributes design judgment across multiple experienced reviewers, on the record, before significant money and engineering time are committed -- catching blind spots and conflicts a single architect's own review can't.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the evaluation domains this lesson describes a well-run ARB systematically checking?
options: Scalability and performance
Security
Integration
The personal popularity of the presenting architect
questions.explain: The lesson lists requirements traceability, scalability, security, integration, data model/quality, governance/maintainability, and risk/tradeoffs as the systematic evaluation domains -- personal popularity isn't one of them and has no place in a real board's evaluation.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say the earliest practical point for an ARB gate is the highest-leverage review point?
options: Because reviewing early is legally required
Because changes are cheapest to make the earlier a review happens relative to when code gets written
Because early reviews don't require any preparation
Because later reviews are always more thorough than early ones
questions.explain: The principle is that the earlier a review happens relative to actual build work, the cheaper it is to act on what the board finds -- a design change costs far less than a rebuild.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what distinguishes a real ARB from a casual hallway design conversation with a senior colleague?
options: An ARB is deliberately convened, has defined evaluators not personally invested in the specific design, produces a documented outcome, and carries actual authority to block the design
There is no real difference -- both serve exactly the same governance function
A hallway conversation is always more rigorous because it's less formal
An ARB never produces a documented outcome, only a passing recommendation
questions.explain: The lesson specifically contrasts deliberate convening, independent evaluators, a documented outcome, and real blocking authority against the informality of a hallway chat -- treating one like the other creates friction in both directions.

questions.q: Per this lesson, why does the course avoid committing to a specific number of minutes or panelists for the Salesforce CTA review board?
options: Because the CTA review board doesn't actually exist
Because Salesforce-ecosystem training sources report these specifics differently and the program's exact format changes over time, so the candidate's own current official guide is the source of truth
Because exact timing and panel size are completely irrelevant to CTA candidates
Because every CTA review board uses a totally different format with no common structure at all
questions.explain: Multiple training sources describe broadly similar phases and panel-based questioning, but exact reported numbers differ and the program evolves over time -- so this lesson hedges on specifics and points to Salesforce's own current official guide, while still teaching the underlying present-and-defend structure that doesn't change.
